The lathe is primarily used for cutting and shaping metal. It consists of various parts including an chuck, tailstock, slide rest, bed, headstock, spindle, cross-slide, handlebar, and lead screw drive.
```
The handlebar connects the workpiece (in the lathe chuck or vice, if required) to the main axis via the lead screws. The lead screw drives are located at both ends; two opposite threads turn together on each side.

Slide rest slides back and forth along the longitudinal direction with respect to the spindle when turned by the handlebars attached to the cross-slide.

Headstock serves as the driving end of the lathe's rotational motion. It includes the bearing box assembly (also known simply as bushing), which fits inside the outer casing to support its rotation, and also contains other rotating mechanisms.

Bed is one of the major components in the lathe. It is supported by the tail stock, where it rotates to facilitate precise adjustments during machining operations.

Spindle refers to the central shaft that runs through the center from one end of the bed to the other. It supports both the sliding rests along their movement within and the lead screws for moving the tool carriage across the slide rest.

Cross-slide adjusts relative positions between the tool holder, spindle, and slide rest. Its design allows for fine control while operating tools mounted on it and enables accurate positioning based on specific requirements.
```
